pages.alt: A 440 V, 60 Hz insulated switchboard: a bus bar, eight feeders F1 to F8 and the hull, joined by an insulation monitor whose needle sits above its 44 kΩ alarm line. Open: F6. The fault is in the pump motor on F6's sub-board, and the pump is running.

pages.name: A jump, not a nudge
pages.task: Say the fault were 20 kΩ instead of solid. The monitor reads 19.1 kΩ. You open F3 and it reads 19.2 kΩ. What does that tell you?
pages.answer: F3 is healthy. Only its own 3 MΩ left the total
pages.why: The 20 kΩ fault is by far the lowest path, so it sets the total. Taking off one healthy 3 MΩ path barely changes it. Look for a jump, not a nudge.

pages.name: Recovered, then healthy
pages.task: You open F5 and the dial recovers to 429 kΩ. You close F5 again, and the dial reads 375 kΩ. What should you suspect?
pages.answer: A faulty load switched off as you opened F5
pages.why: If F5 held the fault, closing it should have brought the alarm back. It did not. So a load left the system at that moment. A pump stopping on its pressure switch is one example. Note what was running, and wait for the alarm to return.

pages.alt: A 440 V, 60 Hz insulated switchboard: a bus bar, eight feeders F1 to F8 and the hull, joined by an insulation monitor whose needle sits below its 44 kΩ alarm line, with the alarm lamp lit. Every breaker is closed. The fault is in the pump motor on F6's sub-board, and the pump is running. At 60 Hz the clamps read F1 575 mA, F2 14.4 mA, F3 14.4 mA, F4 14.4 mA, F5 14.4 mA, F6 661 mA, F7 14.4 mA, F8 14.4 mA.

pages.name: The biggest reading
pages.task: You clamp F1 first, at 60 Hz. It reads 575 mA, far more than the short feeders you have tried. Is F1 the faulty one?
pages.answer: Not proven. A long healthy feeder passes that much
pages.why: At 60 Hz a clamp reads charging current as well as fault current. F6 reads only 86 mA more than F1. A real clamp also picks up a little from load current and unequal cables. A partial fault shrinks every reading too. So a short faulty feeder is hard to tell from a long healthy one by size alone.[^3]

pages.task: The pulse shows on F6. F6 feeds a sub-board with four circuits: Fan, Pump, Heater and Lighting. What will the clamps on those four circuits show?

pages.alt: A 440 V, 60 Hz insulated switchboard: a bus bar, eight feeders F1 to F8 and the hull, joined by an insulation monitor whose needle sits below its 44 kΩ alarm line, with the alarm lamp lit. Every breaker is closed. The fault is in the pump motor on F6's sub-board, and the pump is running. With the pulse injected, the clamps read F1 0 mA, F2 0 mA, F3 0 mA, F4 0 mA, F5 0 mA, F6 10 mA, F7 0 mA, F8 0 mA. On F6's sub-board: incoming 10 mA, Fan 0 mA, Pump 10 mA, Heater 0 mA, Lighting 0 mA.

pages.name: What the monitor cannot see
pages.task: The monitor reads 375 kΩ, well above its 44 kΩ alarm line. F6's pump is stopped, its contactor open. Does the monitor prove the pump's insulation healthy?
pages.answer: No. It cannot see a load that is switched off
pages.why: A monitor reads only what is connected. A switched-off load is out of its reach.[^6] To prove the pump, test it dead, or run it and watch the monitor.

pages.name: The dead test in order
pages.task: Put the steps for the pump circuit's dead test in order.
pages.answer: 1. Isolate the circuit and lock it off. 2. Prove it dead. 3. Disconnect the electronics and any monitor on it. 4. Test at 500 V DC, cores joined, to earth. 5. Split at the terminal box and test each part.
pages.why: Isolation and proof come first, for your safety. The electronics come off next, so the test voltage cannot damage them or skew the reading. Then test the whole circuit, and split it to find which part holds the fault.

pages.name: A fault on the long feeder
pages.task: Suppose the solid fault were on F1, the long feeder, instead of F6. What would F1's clamp read at 60 Hz?
pages.answer: 101 mA, the other seven feeders' charging current
pages.why: The faulty feeder carries every other feeder's charging current home. Seven short feeders of 0.05 µF a line make 0.35 µF. That passes 0.35 × 287 = 101 mA. So faulty F1 reads less than healthy F1 did. A feeder's reading at 60 Hz depends on the rest of the board, not on whether it is faulty.
